s: What is the splitting of a heavy nucleus called?
x: Fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus, while fusion is the joining of two light nuclei.

s: Through which process is all present-day nuclear electricity generated?
x: Present-day reactors use fission; fusion occurs in the Sun and stars and fusion power is still at the R&D stage.

s: How much energy per unit mass does nuclear fusion release compared with nuclear fission?
x: Fusion releases more energy per unit mass than fission, though it needs extremely high temperature and pressure.

s: What initiates the fusion reaction in a hydrogen bomb?
x: A hydrogen bomb uses fusion triggered by a fission explosion; an atomic bomb is based on uncontrolled fission.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: The Hiroshima bomb, Little Boy, used U-235. The Nagasaki bomb, Fat Man, used Pu-239.

s: What is the minimum mass of fissile material that can sustain a chain reaction called?
x: Critical mass is the minimum fissile mass for a chain reaction; criticality is the self-sustaining state itself.

s: The bomb 'Little Boy' dropped on Hiroshima used which fissile material?
x: Little Boy (Hiroshima) used U-235; Fat Man (Nagasaki) used Pu-239.

s: What are ³H and ⁴He, each having two neutrons, called?
x: Nuclides with the same number of neutrons are isotones; ³H and ⁴He both have 2 neutrons.

s: Which element is bombarded with neutrons to produce tritium?
x: Tritium (1 proton + 2 neutrons) is produced by bombarding lithium with neutrons.

s: What are atoms having the same mass number but different atomic numbers called?
x: Isobars share mass number but differ in atomic number; isotopes share atomic number but differ in mass number.

s: Which of the following is wrongly matched?
o: U-238 – Fissile fuel of Stage III and KAMINI
U-233 – Fissile fuel of Stage III and KAMINI
Pu-239 – Fissile isotope produced from U-238 by neutron absorption
U-235 – Fissile isotope present in natural uranium
x: U-238 is the fertile isotope converted into Pu-239; the fuel of Stage III and KAMINI is U-233.

s: What does enrichment of uranium refer to?
o: Removing all radioactive isotopes from natural uranium
Increasing the proportion of U-238 through chemical separation
Increasing the proportion of U-235 through isotope separation
x: Enrichment raises the share of U-235, the fissile isotope, by isotope separation; it does not increase U-238.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a nuclear fuel but may serve as a moderator, coolant or absorber in a reactor?
x: Graphite is a reactor moderator, not a nuclear fuel. U-235, Pu-239 and U-233 are fissile fuels.

s: What percentage of natural uranium is U-235?
x: Fissile U-235 is only 0.72% of natural uranium; fertile U-238 is 99.28%.

s: To what level of U-235 must uranium be enriched for light water reactors?
x: LWRs need 3–5% U-235, above the natural 0.72%.

s: U-238 is a fertile isotope. Into which fissile material is it converted?
x: U-238 absorbs a neutron and becomes fissile Pu-239; Th-232 becomes U-233.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about nuclear isotopes?
x: U-238 is fertile, not fissile; the fissile fuel bred from it is Pu-239.

s: Why is Xenon-135 called a 'nuclear poison'?
x: Xenon-135 absorbs neutrons and so acts as a nuclear poison in a reactor.

s: Which one of the following correctly matches radiation with its usual shielding requirement?
o: Beta — a few millimetres of aluminium
Gamma — a thin layer of aluminium only
x: Beta radiation can generally be stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Alpha is stopped by paper or skin, whereas gamma requires dense shielding such as lead or concrete.

s: The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time required for:
o: Its atomic mass to become zero
Its radiation to lose half its penetrating power
Half of its radioactive nuclei to decay
x: Half-life is the time required for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to undergo decay.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about radioactive series?
o: The neptunium series is a natural radioactive series
The thorium series begins with Th-232 and ends with Pb-208
The actinium series begins with U-235 and ends with Pb-207
The uranium series begins with U-238 and ends with Pb-206
x: The neptunium series is artificial, not natural.

s: What is a positively charged beta particle called?
x: Positive beta is a positron; negative beta is an electron and an alpha particle is a +2 helium nucleus.

s: Which one of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The neutron is a neutral particle.
x: Option A is incorrect: radioactivity is a nuclear process, unaffected by chemical bonding, and it emits alpha, beta and gamma radiation.

s: In which year did Henri Becquerel discover radioactivity?
x: Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896.

s: In which isotope does the natural thorium decay series, starting with Th-232, end?
x: The thorium series runs Th-232 to Pb-208; the uranium series ends in Pb-206, and the neptunium series is artificial.

s: Which of the following stops gamma radiation?
x: Gamma rays need lead or concrete; alpha is stopped by paper and beta by a few mm of aluminium.

s: In Light Water Reactors, which account for over 85% of world nuclear capacity, what role does light water play?
x: LWRs use light water for both moderation and cooling and make up more than 85% of global nuclear capacity.

s: Which component of a nuclear reactor slows down neutrons?
x: The moderator slows neutrons; the coolant carries heat and control rods absorb neutrons.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: BWR — light water as moderator and coolant
AHWR — no moderator and no coolant
x: A BWR uses light water both as moderator and coolant, with the water boiling in the core. PHWRs use heavy water, while FBRs use sodium and no moderator.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Tarapur is associated with BWR technology, whereas Kudankulam uses VVER reactors.

s: Which reactor type has no moderator and uses liquid sodium as coolant?
x: The FBR uses fast neutrons, so it needs no moderator; it is cooled by liquid sodium.

s: Which of the following substances is used in the control rods of a nuclear reactor?
x: Control rods absorb neutrons to control the chain reaction; boron and cadmium are used for them.

s: What is the function of control rods in a nuclear reactor?
o: To absorb neutrons and control the rate of fission
To carry heat to make steam
x: Control rods absorb neutrons and so control the rate of the chain reaction; the moderator slows neutrons.

s:
Consider the following statements about India's nuclear power:
1. NPCIL operates 25 reactors with an operating capacity of 8,880 MW.
2. India's nuclear capacity target is 22.38 GW by 2031-32.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Both figures are correct: 25 reactors with 8,880 MW, and a target of 22.38 GW by 2031-32.

s:
Assertion (A): APSARA research reactor is located at Kalpakkam.
Reason (R): APSARA is a swimming-pool (pool-type) reactor.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: APSARA is located at BARC, Trombay, not Kalpakkam; it is a pool-type reactor that became critical in 1956.

s: With which country's collaboration was the CIRUS research reactor at Trombay built?
x: CIRUS was built with Canada following a 1956 decision and was shut down in 2010.

s:
Arrange the following research reactors in ascending order of capacity:
1. Dhruva
2. KAMINI
3. CIRUS
x: KAMINI is 30 kW, CIRUS 40 MW and Dhruva, India's largest research reactor, 100 MW.

s: Which is India's largest research reactor?
x: Dhruva (100 MW) at Trombay is the largest; APSARA was the first.

s: Where is KAMINI, the world's only U-233-fuelled reactor, located?
x: KAMINI (30 kW) is at IGCAR, Kalpakkam.

s: Which was the first research reactor of India and of Asia?
x: Apsara at BARC, Trombay, a pool-type reactor, was India's first and Asia's first research reactor.

s: In which year did Apsara, India's first research reactor, attain criticality?
x: Apsara at Trombay went critical in 1956; it was Indian-built.

s: On which reactor design are NPCIL's proposed Bharat Small Reactors based?
x: NPCIL sought proposals for 220 MW PHWR-based Bharat Small Reactors as captive plants for industry.

s: What is the refuelling interval of Small Modular Reactors?
x: SMRs are generally factory-built with a refuelling interval of about 3–7 years, longer than conventional reactors.

s: Which of the following pairs is wrongly matched?
x: IGCAR is at Kalpakkam, where it works on FBR technology and its fuel cycle; AMD is the Hyderabad body.

s: What is the maximum capacity per unit of a Small Modular Reactor (SMR)?
x: An SMR has a capacity of up to 300 MWe per unit, about one-third the size of a conventional reactor.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: BHAVINI — Mumbai — uranium mining and milling
BARC — Trombay — research and development in nuclear technologies
UCIL — Jaduguda — uranium mining and milling
x: BHAVINI is located at Kalpakkam and is associated with fast breeder reactors. Uranium mining and milling is the role of UCIL at Jaduguda.

s: To what did the Atomic Energy Act of 1948 mainly limit atomic energy in India?
x: The Atomic Energy Act, 1948, limited the use of atomic energy to peaceful purposes.

s: The SHANTI Act 2025 is associated with which of the following developments?
o: It restricts nuclear power generation exclusively to government companies.
It transfers all nuclear research from BARC to IIT Hyderabad.
It abolishes the Nuclear Energy Mission and the three-stage programme.
It repeals the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010, enabling licensed private participation.
x: The SHANTI Act 2025 repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010, allowing licensed private companies and joint ventures to build, own and operate nuclear plants.

s: What nuclear power capacity does the Nuclear Energy Mission (Union Budget 2025-26) target by 2047?
x: The mission targets 100 GW by 2047, with Rs 20,000 crore for Small Modular Reactors.

s: In which year was AEET, set up in 1954, renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre?
x: BARC began in 1954 as AEET and was renamed in 1967 after Homi Bhabha.

s: Which nuclear body–seat pair is correctly matched?
x: AMD (atomic minerals exploration) and NFC are at Hyderabad; UCIL is at Jaduguda and IGCAR at Kalpakkam.

s: In which year was the Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) established?
x: IGCAR at Kalpakkam was set up in 1971 for FBR technology.

s: The Nuclear Energy Mission (Budget 2025-26) earmarks how much for Small Modular Reactors?
x: The Mission sets ₹20,000 crore for SMRs and a target of 100 GW by 2047.

s: The SHANTI Act 2025 repealed the CLNDA 2010 and which other law?
x: SHANTI repealed the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and CLNDA 2010, not the 1948 Act.

s: In which year was the Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) set up?
x: The DAE was set up in 1954; the Atomic Energy Act came in 1948.

s: CODENE, a centre for Small Modular Reactor design and safety, has been set up at which institution?
x: CODENE at IIT Hyderabad works on SMR design and safety (June 2026).

s: India possesses about what share of the world's thorium?
x: India has about 25% of global thorium (and about 2% of uranium).

s: Which one of the following correctly represents the sequence of India's three-stage nuclear power programme?
x: India's programme begins with PHWRs using natural uranium, proceeds to FBRs using plutonium-based fuel, and culminates in thorium-based AHWRs or other thorium reactors.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Homi Bhabha's three-stage nuclear programme?
o: It aims at self-reliance through a closed fuel cycle
It seeks to overcome India's scarcity of uranium
It makes use of India's abundant thorium
It was designed to use abundant uranium in place of scarce thorium
x: The programme uses abundant thorium to overcome scarce uranium, not the other way round.

s: The AHWR acts as a bridge between which stages of India's nuclear programme?
x: The AHWR bridges Stage I and Stage III, advancing thorium use without passing through Stage II.

s: The 300 MW Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) designed by BARC uses which fuel combination?
x: The AHWR is a 300 MW thorium reactor with heavy-water moderator, boiling light-water coolant and Th-232 + U-233 fuel.

s: On which reactors is Stage I of India's three-stage nuclear programme based?
x: Stage I uses PHWRs fuelled by natural uranium; its spent fuel yields Pu-239 for the next stage.

s: With which material does ANEEL fuel, developed by the US firm Clean Core Thorium Energy, combine thorium?
x: ANEEL is thorium plus HALEU and can be used in existing PHWRs.

s: Which of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: AHWR — reactor already built and operating at Trombay
x: AHWR is a BARC design for a 300 MW thorium reactor; it is not described as an already built and operating reactor at Trombay. The other pairs are correct.

s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a bottleneck affecting the progression towards Stage III?
o: Absence of any thorium resources in India
x: The identified bottlenecks include a thin fissile inventory for Stage III, 10–12-year construction periods and local protests. Absence of thorium resources is not identified as a bottleneck; the programme is based on India's abundant thorium.

s: Who is known as the 'Father of the Indian nuclear programme'?
x: Homi J. Bhabha planned the three-stage programme in the 1950s and is its father.

s: Stage II of India's three-stage nuclear programme uses which fuel?
x: Stage II FBRs burn MOX of Pu-239 and U-238; Stage I uses natural uranium and Stage III thorium with U-233.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR)?
o: It is a conceptual prototype designed at BARC
It is regarded as India's flagship thorium reactor
It uses liquid sodium as its coolant
It uses heavy water as its moderator
x: The AHWR is a BARC-designed thorium reactor that uses heavy water as moderator and boiling light water as coolant. Liquid sodium is the coolant of fast breeder reactors, not of the AHWR.

s: What is the designed capacity of the thorium-based Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) of BARC?
x: The AHWR is a 300 MWe (920 MWth) thorium-based design of BARC, not yet built.

s: Which body is permitted to process and export monazite in India?
x: Only government bodies such as IREL may process and export monazite, found in the beach sands of Kerala and Odisha.

s: Jaduguda, India's first uranium mine, is located in which district and State?
x: Jaduguda is located in East Singhbhum district of Jharkhand and is India's first uranium mine.

s: The Tummalapalle uranium mine of UCIL is located in which district of Andhra Pradesh?
x: Tummalapalle, a UCIL uranium mine with a processing plant, is in YSR Kadapa district.

s: Approximately what proportion of India's imported uranium comes from Kazakhstan?
x: About 80 percent of imported uranium is stated to come from Kazakhstan.

s: Thorium is considered advantageous over uranium because it:
o: Can be used directly in every reactor without conversion
Is more abundant, yields more energy per unit mass of mined mineral and produces less harmful waste
Requires no reactor or fuel-cycle technology
Is less abundant but produces no energy waste
x: Thorium is more abundant, provides greater energy per unit mass of mined mineral and leaves less harmful waste compared with uranium.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about monazite?
o: It is the principal ore of thorium
It contains rare earths such as lanthanum and cerium
Only IREL-type government bodies may process and export it
It occurs along the entire Indian coast
x: Monazite occurs in beach sands of Kerala, TN, Odisha, AP and others, not along the entire coast.

s: India holds about what share of the world's uranium?
x: India has about 2% of world uranium against about 25% of thorium.

s: What is India's rank in the world in thorium reserves?
x: India holds about 25% of world thorium and has the third-largest thorium reserve.

s: Beach placer sands rich in monazite are found along the coasts of which of the following States?
o: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
x: Monazite (thorium ore) occurs in beach sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and West Bengal, not the entire coast.

s: Besides thorium, which of the following is obtained from monazite?
o: Rare earths such as lanthanum and cerium
x: Monazite is the principal thorium ore and also gives rare earths (lanthanum, cerium), phosphate and a little uranium.

s: Which coolant is used in the Stage II Fast Breeder Reactors of India?
x: Stage II FBRs use liquid sodium coolant and no moderator, since fast neutrons are needed.

s: The criticality of the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor in April 2026 signified entry into which stage of India's three-stage nuclear programme?
x: PFBR criticality in April 2026 marked India's entry into Stage II of the three-stage programme.

s: What was the 2005 milestone associated with IGCAR and the Fast Breeder Test Reactor?
x: IGCAR’s 2005 milestone was the reprocessing of the mixed-carbide fuel used in the Fast Breeder Test Reactor.

s: Into which fissile material do fast neutrons convert the U-238 blanket in a fast breeder reactor?
x: Fast neutrons turn the U-238 blanket into Pu-239, so the FBR breeds more fuel than it consumes.

s: What is the rated electrical capacity of the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam?
x: The sodium-cooled, pool-type PFBR is rated at 500 MWe (1,250 MWt).

s: Once the PFBR operates commercially, India is expected to become the second country after which country to operate a commercial-scale fast breeder reactor?
x: India is expected to become the second country after Russia to operate a commercial-scale fast breeder reactor.

s: Which cost and schedule difficulties has the PFBR project faced?
o: Its cost was halved and it finished 5 years early.
Its cost doubled and it ran 16 years late.
Its cost tripled and it ran 30 years late.
Its cost remained unchanged and it ran 2 years late.
x: The PFBR's cost was reported to have doubled, while the project ran 16 years late.

s: In which year did the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) at Kalpakkam first attain criticality?
x: The FBTR, based on the French Rapsodie design, went critical on 18 October 1985.

s: Which institution designed the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam?
o: Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR)
x: IGCAR, Kalpakkam designed the PFBR; BHAVINI built and commissioned it.

s: BHAVINI, a public sector undertaking of the Department of Atomic Energy set up in 2003, builds and operates which type of reactors?
x: BHAVINI was set up to build and run fast breeder reactors such as the PFBR at Kalpakkam.

s: The design of the Fast Breeder Test Reactor (FBTR) at Kalpakkam is based on which French reactor?
x: FBTR, critical in 1985, was designed on the lines of the French fast reactor Rapsodie.

s: The Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor is significant because it is:
o: India's first indigenous Fast Breeder Reactor
x: PFBR is described as India's first indigenous Fast Breeder Reactor.

s: ITER is designed to give about 500 MW of output from how much input power?
x: ITER, a tokamak fusion device, is designed for 500 MW output from 50 MW input, about ten times more out than in.

s: Where are India's tokamaks Aditya and SST-1 located?
x: Aditya (India's first tokamak) and SST-1 are at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar, not BARC.

s: Which component of ITER does India supply?
x: India, a member since 2005, supplies the cryostat.

s: Where is the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (ITER) being constructed?
o: Lawrence Livermore in the United Kingdom
x: ITER is located at Cadarache in southern France. Gandhinagar is associated with India's Institute for Plasma Research.

s: In which year did India join the ITER project?
x: India joined ITER in 2005 and supplies its cryostat.

s:
Consider the following statements about ITER:
1. It is a tokamak based on magnetic confinement.
2. Canada is one of its members.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: ITER at Cadarache is a magnetic-confinement tokamak; its members are the EU, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Russia and USA, not Canada.

s: Where was the first fusion ignition with net energy gain achieved in December 2022?
o: National Ignition Facility, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, USA
x: The National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore (USA) achieved fusion ignition using lasers in December 2022.

s: Which was the first Indian tokamak?
x: Aditya, at the Institute for Plasma Research, Gandhinagar, was India's first tokamak; SST-1 came later.

s: Which nuclear power station has India's first fully indigenous PHWRs and is also associated with the PFBR?
x: Kalpakkam's MAPS units are the first fully indigenous PHWRs, and the site is associated with the PFBR.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about firsts in India's nuclear power programme?
o: Tarapur began operation in 1960 with two PHWRs
Tarapur went into operation in 1969 with two BWRs
RAPS-1, the first PHWR, was built with AECL of Canada and started in 1972
Jaitapur, with a planned 9,900 MW, is the largest planned nuclear project
x: Tarapur, India's first nuclear power plant, started in 1969 with two boiling water reactors, not in 1960 with PHWRs.

s: Which one of the following is NOT correctly matched?
x: Narora uses PHWRs, not VVER reactors. Gorakhpur is in Haryana, Kudankulam is in Tamil Nadu, and Kovvada is proposed in Andhra Pradesh.

s: In which State is KAPP-3, India's first indigenous 700 MW PHWR, located?
x: KAPP-3 is at Kakrapar in Gujarat and began commercial operation on 30 June 2023.

s: The Rawatbhata (RAPS/RAPP) atomic power station, India's oldest PHWR site, is located in which State?
x: Rawatbhata (RAPS/RAPP) is in Rajasthan; its Canada-assisted RAPS-1 began in 1972 and RAPP-7 (700 MW) now operates. Kakrapar is in Gujarat, Chutka (planned) in Madhya Pradesh and Narora in Uttar Pradesh.

s: Which nuclear project–State pair is correctly matched?
x: Kaiga is in Karnataka; Chutka is in Madhya Pradesh, Mahi Banswara in Rajasthan and Gorakhpur in Haryana.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about milestones in India's nuclear power programme?
o: RAPS-1 was the first PHWR in India
KAPP-3 was the first PHWR in India
Nangal housed the first Heavy Water Plant
MAPS was the first fully indigenous PHWR
x: KAPP-3 was India's first 700 MW unit; the first PHWR was RAPS-1.

s: Who is building the Mahi Banswara nuclear power project?
x: Mahi Banswara is being developed by ASHVINI (Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Limited), an NPCIL–NTPC joint venture.

s: What did the Government of India sanction in 'fleet mode' in 2017?
x: The 2017 fleet-mode sanction covered ten 700 MW PHWRs (Kaiga 5-6, Gorakhpur 3-4, Chutka 1-2 and Mahi Banswara 1-4). Six EPRs are the French-assisted Jaitapur plan, VVERs are the Russian units at Kudankulam, and the 2 x 500 MWe FBRs are the follow-on to PFBR at Kalpakkam.

s: In which State is the Gorakhpur (GHAVP) nuclear power project located?
x: Gorakhpur NPP is in Haryana; Narora is the plant in Uttar Pradesh.

s: The Narora atomic power station is in which State?
x: Narora (2 x 220 MW PHWR, Seismic Zone IV) is in Uttar Pradesh.

s: Which nuclear power station is located near the Kali river in Uttara Kannada?
x: Kaiga (4 units, 880 MW) in Karnataka is near the Kali river.

s: Fleet-mode construction of nuclear reactors aims to cut the construction period from how many years to how many?
x: Fleet-mode construction aims to reduce the build time from 13 years to 8 years.

s: The standard sizes of India's PHWR units have grown in which order?
x: PHWR unit sizes went 220 → 540 → 700 MW, all indigenised.

s: In which State is Chutka 1-2, among the fleet-mode 700 MW PHWRs, located?
x: Chutka is in Madhya Pradesh; Mahi Banswara is in Rajasthan and Kaiga 5-6 in Karnataka.

s: Besides Caesium-137, which material from medical or industrial sources is typical for a dirty bomb?
x: Caesium-137 and Cobalt-60 are the typical dirty-bomb materials; U-235 in a reactor core is not included.

s: Which Nuclear Security Summit–year pair is correctly matched?
x: The summits were Washington 2010, Seoul 2012, The Hague 2014 and Washington 2016, the last.

s: Which organisation holds the International Conference on Nuclear Security (ICONS), a ministerial conference?
x: ICONS is the IAEA's ministerial International Conference on Nuclear Security.

s: Which one of the following is correctly matched with its INES rating?
x: Three Mile Island was rated Level 5. Chernobyl and Fukushima Daiichi were Level 7, while Kashiwazaki-Kariwa was classified as a minor event.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: The Three Mile Island accident occurred in 1979 in the USA.
The Fukushima Daiichi disaster occurred in 2010 in Japan.
The Mayapuri incident involved an orphan Cobalt-60 source.
The Chernobyl disaster occurred on 26 April 1986.
x: Option B is incorrect: the Fukushima Daiichi disaster, set off by a tsunami, happened in 2011, not 2010, and was rated INES Level 7. Chernobyl was on 26 April 1986.

s:
Assertion (A): Chernobyl and Fukushima Daiichi were both rated Level 7 on the INES.
Reason (R): The Mayapuri radiological incident occurred in Delhi in 2010.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true, but the Mayapuri incident has no bearing on the INES rating of Chernobyl and Fukushima.

s: Which of the following nuclear accidents is wrongly matched?
x: The Three Mile Island partial core meltdown in the USA occurred in 1979, not 1986.

s: What is a dirty bomb?
o: A reactor meltdown caused by loss of coolant
A missile carrying a thermonuclear warhead
A conventional explosive that disperses radioactive material
A nuclear weapon producing a sustained chain reaction
x: A dirty bomb, or radiological dispersal device, uses a conventional explosion to spread radioactive material.

s: In which country did the Three Mile Island accident (1979) take place?
x: Three Mile Island was in Pennsylvania, USA, in 1979.

s: Where is the GCNEP, announced by India at the 2010 Nuclear Security Summit, now located?
x: India announced the Global Centre for Nuclear Energy Partnership in 2010; it is at Bahadurgarh.

s: At what level was the Three Mile Island accident rated on the INES scale?
x: Three Mile Island was level 5; only Chernobyl and Fukushima are level 7.

s: In which country did the SL-1 nuclear accident of 1961 take place?
x: The SL-1 accident took place in Idaho, USA, in 1961.

s: In which State is the Thal heavy water plant located?
x: Thal is in Maharashtra, not Gujarat; Nangal is in Punjab and Talcher in Odisha.

s: Which one of the following heavy water plants was commissioned in 1962?
x: Nangal in Punjab was the first heavy water plant and was commissioned in 1962.

s: Manuguru heavy water plant is presently located in which State?
x: Manuguru was in undivided Andhra Pradesh when established, but it is presently in Telangana.

s: Which one of the following is the largest heavy water plant in India?
x: Manuguru is identified as India's largest heavy water plant.

s: Where is the Heavy Water Board, under which all heavy water plants in India function, located?
x: The Heavy Water Board, under DAE, is at Trombay, Mumbai.

s:
Arrange the following heavy water plants in the chronological order of their commissioning:
1. Manuguru
2. Nangal
3. Thal
4. Talcher
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Nangal 1962, Talcher 1985, Thal 1987 and Manuguru 1991.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Heavy water plant)
A. Talcher
B. Thal
C. Kota
D. Manuguru
List-II (State)
1. Maharashtra
2. Telangana
3. Odisha
4. Rajasthan
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: Talcher is in Odisha, Thal in Maharashtra, Kota (Rawatbhata) in Rajasthan and Manuguru in Telangana.

s: In which year did India's Additional Protocol with the IAEA, signed in 2009, come into force?
x: India signed the Additional Protocol in 2009 and it came into force in 2014; it covers only declared civilian facilities.

s: What did India do under the 2006 separation plan linked to the Indo-US nuclear deal?
o: Placed all its nuclear facilities, including military ones, under IAEA safeguards
Separated civil and military facilities and placed civil reactors under IAEA safeguards
Signed the NPT as a non-nuclear-weapon state
Shut down all its research reactors at Trombay
x: In 2006 India separated civil and military facilities and put its civil reactors under IAEA safeguards so that NSG members could supply fuel. Military facilities stayed outside safeguards, India has never signed the NPT, and the research reactors were not all shut by this plan.

s: Where is the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), founded in 1957, headquartered?
x: The IAEA is headquartered at Vienna, Austria; India is a founding member.

s: To which body may the IAEA report non-compliance with safeguards obligations?
x: The IAEA can report safeguards non-compliance to the United Nations Security Council.

s: When did India sign the India-Specific Safeguards Agreement with the IAEA?
x: The India-Specific Safeguards Agreement was signed on 2 February 2009.

s:
Consider the following statements about the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA):
1. It was founded in 1957 and is headquartered at Vienna.
2. India is a founding member of the IAEA.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The IAEA was founded in 1957 with HQ at Vienna, Austria, and India is one of its founding members.

s: The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG), which takes decisions by consensus, has how many members?
x: The NSG has 48 members, works by consensus and has no permanent secretariat.

s: On which policy is India's nuclear doctrine based?
o: First Use only against non-nuclear states
x: India follows a No First Use policy; it is not a party to the TPNW.

s: The Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG), popularly known as the ‘London Club’, was formed in response to which event?
o: The signing of the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty
x: The NSG was formed in 1975, in response to India’s 1974 Pokhran-I nuclear test.

s: In which year did the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), which India has never signed, enter into force?
x: The NPT dates from 1968 and entered into force in 1970; India has never signed it.

s: India has not signed the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) mainly because it objects to which of the following features?
o: The absence of any reference to nuclear disarmament
The absence of time-bound nuclear disarmament and the continued possibility of subcritical tests
The recognition of only five nuclear-weapon states
The treaty’s restriction of only atmospheric tests
x: India has not signed the CTBT because it does not provide for time-bound nuclear disarmament and still permits subcritical tests.

s: In which year did the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW) enter into force?
x: The TPNW entered into force in 2021; India has not signed it, holding that it adds nothing to customary law.

s: India’s application for membership of the Nuclear Suppliers Group was made in which year, and which country has mainly blocked its entry?
x: India applied for NSG membership in 2016. China has mainly blocked India’s entry, particularly because India is not a party to the NPT.

s: Which one of the following would NOT follow from India's membership of the Nuclear Suppliers Group?
o: Participation in the export-control decision process
Access to the latest nuclear technology
x: NSG membership could provide access to advanced technology and a say in rule-making, but it would not make India an NPT member.

s:
Arrange the following Indian memberships of international export-control regimes in chronological order:
A. Australia Group
B. Missile Technology Control Regime
C. Wassenaar Arrangement
x: India joined the MTCR in 2016, the Wassenaar Arrangement in 2017 and the Australia Group in 2018.

s: Which of these nuclear treaties has India signed?
x: India signed the PTBT (1963); it has not signed the NPT, CTBT or TPNW.

s: In which year was the Nuclear Suppliers Group (NSG) formed?
x: The NSG ('London Club') was formed in 1975 in response to India's Pokhran-I test of 1974.

s: Which is India's second-largest operating nuclear power plant, at 1,840 MW?
x: Kakrapar is the second-largest operating plant at 1,840 MW; Jaitapur (9,900 MW) is the largest planned plant.

s: Who developed the 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam?
o: Bhabha Atomic Research Centre's Dhruva unit
x: PFBR is developed by BHAVINI (APPSC-G1 2024 key) and designed by IGCAR; NPCIL holds equity in BHAVINI. ASHVINI is the NPCIL-NTPC joint venture building Mahi Banswara, AERB is the regulator, and Dhruva is a BARC research reactor.

s: In which year was the Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) registered?
x: NPCIL, a public sector enterprise under the DAE, was registered in September 1987.

s: What is India's installed nuclear power capacity in 2026?
x: Installed nuclear capacity is about 8.78 GW (8,780 MW) from 24 NPCIL reactors. 1.62 is the percentage share of installed power capacity, 22.38 GW is the 2031-32 target, and 54 GW is NPCIL's share of the 100 GW 2047 goal.

s: What was the share of nuclear power in India's total electricity generation in 2024–25?
x: Nuclear power accounted for 3.1% of electricity generation in 2024–25. The 1.62% figure refers to its share of installed capacity.

s: The Nuclear Energy Mission envisages India's nuclear power capacity reaching approximately what level by 2047?
x: The Nuclear Energy Mission targets 100 GW of nuclear capacity by 2047.

s: How much nuclear capacity is NPCIL expected to add under the 2047 target?
x: NPCIL is expected to add 54 GW as part of the effort to reach the 100 GW target by 2047.

s: What is nuclear power's share of India's installed power capacity?
x: Nuclear is 1.62% of installed capacity but about 3.1% of generation.

s: Which country was the top nuclear-power generator in 2024?
x: The USA led, followed by China, France, Russia and South Korea; France gets the largest share of its electricity from nuclear.

s: What record nuclear generation did India achieve in FY2024-25?
x: Generation reached 56.681 BU, the first time above 50 BU.

s: Which country gets the largest share of its electricity from nuclear power?
x: The USA generates the most nuclear power, but France gets the largest share of its electricity from nuclear.

s: Which country supplies approximately 80 per cent of India's uranium imports?
x: Kazakhstan supplies approximately 80 per cent of India's uranium imports.

s: In which year did India sign its civil nuclear agreement with Japan?
x: The India-Japan civil nuclear agreement dates to 2016; France's was of 30 September 2008 and Australia's of 2014.

s: The India-US 123 Agreement is named after Section 123 of which law?
x: The name comes from Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954; the agreement was signed under Manmohan Singh and George W. Bush.

s: The NSG waiver of September 2008 ended how many years of India's exclusion from nuclear trade?
x: The 2008 waiver ended 34 years of exclusion and allowed civil nuclear trade.

s: In which year was India's civil nuclear agreement with Australia signed?
x: The India–Australia deal was signed in 2014 and came into force in 2015.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (Country)
A. France
B. Australia
C. Japan
List-II (Year of civil nuclear agreement with India)
1. 2016
2. 2014
3. 2008
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: France signed the first post-waiver deal in 2008, Australia in 2014 and Japan in 2016.

s: The India-US civil nuclear (123) Agreement of 2008 was concluded during the tenure of which leaders?
o: Atal Bihari Vajpayee and Bill Clinton
Manmohan Singh and George W. Bush
x: The 123 Agreement (2008) is linked with PM Manmohan Singh and President George W. Bush.

s: What is Kashiwazaki-Kariwa known as?
o: the first nuclear plant in India
the world's oldest nuclear power plant
the world's largest nuclear power plant by capacity
the only Level 7 nuclear accident site
x: Kashiwazaki-Kariwa in Japan is the world's largest nuclear power plant by capacity.

s: The Kovvada nuclear project is proposed to use which reactors?
o: AP1000 reactors from the United States
x: Kovvada is proposed to use AP1000 reactors from the United States.

s: Which type of reactor capacity will the VVER units being added at Kudankulam increase for India?
x: The VVER units at Kudankulam add imported light-water reactor capacity to India’s nuclear fleet.

s: Kudankulam Nuclear Power Plant uses which reactor technology and foreign collaboration?
x: Kudankulam uses Russian VVER pressurised water reactors (PWRs).

s: Jaitapur Nuclear Power Project is associated with which combination?
o: Maharashtra, France, EDF and six EPR units
Andhra Pradesh, USA, Westinghouse and six AP1000 units
Tamil Nadu, Russia, Rosatom and six VVER units
Gujarat, Canada, AECL and six PHWR units
x: Jaitapur is located in Maharashtra and is associated with France's EDF and six EPR units.

s: Which is the largest planned nuclear power project in India?
x: Jaitapur (6 EPRs, 9,900 MW) is the largest planned; Kudankulam (2,000 MW) is the largest operating.

s: When was the Industrial Way Forward Agreement relating to Jaitapur signed between NPCIL and EDF?
x: NPCIL and France's EDF signed the Industrial Way Forward Agreement for Jaitapur in March 2018.

s: In which year was the India–USSR agreement for the Kudankulam project signed?
x: The India-USSR agreement associated with Kudankulam was signed in 1988.

s: What is the present status of the Kovvada nuclear power project?
x: Kovvada is at the pre-construction stage; Westinghouse had yet to submit its techno-commercial offer (Nov 2024).

s: How many AP1000 reactors are proposed at Kovvada?
x: Kovvada is to have six AP1000 PWRs by Westinghouse, USA.

s: Besides civil-society protests, which event delayed the Kudankulam nuclear project?
o: The signing of the India-US 123 Agreement
x: The breakup of the USSR and civil-society protests are counted among the delays; the 1991 economic crisis is not.

s: The Kudankulam plant's two running units are of which reactor type?
x: Kudankulam runs 2 x VVER-1000 (Russia); Jaitapur is to have EPRs and Kovvada AP1000s.

s: Ranastalam in Srikakulam district of Andhra Pradesh is the proposed site of which nuclear power project?
x: The Kovvada project (six AP1000 reactors with the USA) is proposed at Ranastalam, Srikakulam.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB)?
o: It licenses nuclear power plants and fuel-cycle facilities
It does not regulate radiation safety in medical and industrial applications
It inspects facilities and can suspend or revoke licences
It regulates management and transport of radioactive waste
x: The AERB does regulate radiation safety in medical and industrial applications, along with licensing, inspection and waste regulation.

s: In which year did the Convention on Nuclear Safety, adopted in 1994, enter into force?
x: The Convention was adopted in 1994 and came into force in 1996; India is a party to it.

s: What is the occupational dose limit for radiation workers, averaged over five years?
x: The limit is 20 mSv a year averaged over five years, with a maximum of 30 mSv in any one year and 100 mSv cumulative.

s: What is the design approach that uses multiple successive layers of protection in nuclear safety called?
x: Defence in Depth is the nuclear-safety design approach based on multiple successive and independent protective layers.

s: What does the Emergency Planning Zone (EPZ) consist of?
o: A single exclusion area of 1–1.5 km around a reactor
A network of specialised centres for detection and response
A district-level command structure led by the District Collector
x: The Emergency Planning Zone is a set of concentric zones around a plant for planning protective actions. The 1–1.5 km exclusion area is only its inner part.

s:
Consider the following statements about the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB):
1. It was set up on 15 November 1983 by an executive order under the Atomic Energy Act, 1962.
2. It got statutory status when the Nuclear Safety Regulatory Authority Bill was enacted.
3. It got statutory status under the SHANTI Act, 2025.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The AERB was created by executive order in 1983; the NSRA Bill was never enacted and statutory status came with the SHANTI Act, 2025.

s: Which radiation-protection principle requires exposure to be kept 'As Low As Reasonably Achievable'?
x: ALARA is the principle requiring exposure to ionising radiation to be kept As Low As Reasonably Achievable.

s: What is the radius of the exclusion zone, with no public habitation, around an Indian nuclear reactor?
x: The exclusion zone is 1–1.5 km (APPSC 2022 key: 1 km); 16 km is the Emergency Planning Zone.

s: Under which body did the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) work before it got statutory status?
o: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
x: The AERB, set up in 1983 by executive order, worked under the DAE, the promoter of nuclear power, which raised the independence debate.

s: What is the radius of the Emergency Planning Zone around an Indian nuclear reactor?
x: The exclusion zone is 1-1.5 km; the Emergency Planning Zone extends to 16 km.

s: Over which activities does the Government retain control under the SHANTI Act, 2025?
o: Spent-fuel reprocessing and heavy-water production only
Enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and heavy-water production
x: The Government retains control over all three: enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and heavy-water production.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act (CLNDA), 2010?
o: Section 17(b) gave the operator a right of recourse against suppliers
The Indian Nuclear Insurance Pool was created to cover suppliers
It capped operator liability at Rs 1,500 crore
x: CLNDA made operator liability no-fault, capped at Rs 1,500 crore with the Centre paying beyond the cap.

s: Along with the Atomic Energy Act, 1962, which law did the SHANTI Act, 2025 repeal?
o: Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010
x: The SHANTI Act repealed the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the CLNDA, 2010; it only amended Section 4 of the Patents Act.

s: What is the liability cap for small modular reactors under the SHANTI Act, 2025?
x: The graded caps are ₹3,000 crore for large facilities, ₹1,500 crore for medium facilities and ₹100 crore for SMRs.

s: At what amount does the SHANTI Act, 2025 cap total nuclear liability?
x: Total liability is capped at 300 million SDR (about Rs 3,900 crore); the excess is met through a Nuclear Liability Fund.

s: In August 2026, the Supreme Court issued notice to the Union and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board in connection with a petition challenging which aspect of the SHANTI framework?
o: Its target of 100 GW nuclear capacity by 2047
x: In August 2026 a Supreme Court Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant issued notice on a petition challenging the liability caps under the SHANTI Act, 2025.

s: At what amount was operator liability capped under the CLNDA 2010?
x: CLNDA capped no-fault operator liability at ₹1,500 crore, with the Centre paying beyond it.

s: Which section of the CLNDA 2010 gave the operator a right of recourse against suppliers?
x: Section 17(b) gave recourse against suppliers; Section 46 kept other civil laws open.

s: To which tribunal do appeals under the SHANTI Act, 2025 lie?
x: Appeals under the SHANTI Act, 2025 go to APTEL.

s: Under the SHANTI Act, 2025, what is the cap on FDI in nuclear power companies?
x: The SHANTI Act lets Indian private firms and JVs build and run plants; foreign firms are excluded and FDI is capped at 49%.

s: Which one of the following radioisotopes is supplied by BRIT as sodium iodide for the diagnosis and treatment of thyroid disorders?
x: Iodine-131 emits beta and gamma radiation and is supplied by BRIT as sodium iodide for thyroid diagnosis and treatment.

s: Which is the most widely used diagnostic radioisotope?
x: Technetium-99m is the most widely used diagnostic isotope, used to image the heart, brain, bones and lungs.

s: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
x: Arsenic-74 emits positrons and is used for locating brain tumours. Iron-59 concerns iron metabolism, Sodium-24 concerns blood flow, and Carbon-14 is used for dating organic material.

s: Radioimmunoassay is used to measure minute quantities of what in blood?
x: Radioimmunoassay uses radioisotopes to measure minute quantities of hormones, enzymes and drugs in blood.

s: What is Iron-59 used to study in medicine?
x: Iron-59 is used for iron metabolism studies.

s: Which radioisotope – radiation emitted pair is correctly matched?
x: I-131 emits beta and gamma; P-32 emits beta, As-74 positrons and Co-60 powerful gamma.

s: Which of the following is Sodium-24 mainly used to study?
x: Sodium-24 emits gamma radiation and is used in blood-flow and circulation studies; it can also help detect pipeline leaks.

s: What is Arsenic-74, a positron emitter, used to locate?
x: As-74 locates brain tumours; I-131 is for thyroid and Na-24 for blood flow and clots.

s: For what is Gold-198 used in medicine?
x: Gold-198 is used in cancer treatment, not for retinal disorders.

s: SPECT imaging generally uses which radioisotope?
x: SPECT uses single gamma emitters, chiefly Technetium-99m; PET uses positron emitters such as F-18 FDG.

s: What does brachytherapy involve, unlike teletherapy?
o: An external Co-60 beam from a distant unit
Injecting F-18 FDG to detect positrons
Placing a sealed radiation source inside or next to the tumour
x: Brachytherapy places a sealed source (e.g. Ir-192 or I-125 seeds) inside or next to the tumour; teletherapy is external-beam, commonly Co-60.

s: Which of the following is primarily used as a positron emitter in PET imaging?
x: PET mainly uses the positron emitter F-18 FDG. Tc-99m is commonly associated with SPECT, while Co-60 is used in teletherapy.

s: What does the 30 MeV Medical Cyclotron at Kolkata produce commercially?
x: The Kolkata Medical Cyclotron produces F-18 FDG commercially for PET imaging.

s: The Tata Memorial Centre is the Anchor Centre for which IAEA initiative?
x: Tata Memorial Centre is the Anchor Centre for the International Atomic Energy Agency’s ‘Rays of Hope’ initiative.

s: Which radioisotope is typically used in teletherapy, an external-beam radiotherapy?
x: Teletherapy uses an external Co-60 beam; Ir-192 and I-125 are brachytherapy sources and F-18 is for PET.

s: Which radioactive noble gas is used in the treatment of cancer?
x: Radon is a radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about radiometric dating?
o: Carbon-14 dating is used mainly for volcanic rocks older than a billion years
U-238 to Pb-206 dating is used for the oldest rocks and the age of the Earth
K-40 to Ar-40 dating is used for volcanic rocks and fossil-bearing layers
Carbon-14 dating covers once-living remains up to about 50,000 years
x: Carbon-14 (half-life about 5,730 years) dates once-living organic remains up to about 50,000 years, not ancient volcanic rocks.

s: Which dating method is used for volcanic rocks and fossil-bearing layers?
x: Potassium-argon dating suits volcanic rocks; Carbon-14 dates only once-living remains.

s: What is the half-life of Carbon-14?
x: C-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years; 50,000 years is the upper limit of what it can date.

s: Who pioneered uranium-lead dating, used to find the age of the Earth?
x: Clair Cameron Patterson pioneered uranium-lead dating; Stadler is known for induced mutation.

s: Up to how many years can Carbon-14 dating date once-living remains?
x: C-14 dates fossils, wood and bones up to about 50,000 years.

s: What type of emitter is radon, formed by the decay of radium?
x: Radon is an alpha emitter produced by radium decay.

s: Long-term inhalation of radon gas is chiefly linked to which disease?
x: Prolonged inhalation of radon, an alpha emitter, causes lung cancer.

s:
Consider the following statements about radon:
1. It can be released from building materials such as granite, brick and concrete.
2. It is a positron emitter used in PET imaging.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Radon comes from soil gas, building materials and uranium mill tailings; it is an alpha emitter, while PET uses positron emitters like F-18.

s:
Consider the following statements about radon:
1. It is a radioactive noble gas used in cancer treatment.
2. Long inhalation of radon can cause lung cancer.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Radon is a radioactive noble gas used to treat cancer, and long inhalation of this alpha emitter causes lung cancer.

s: Which radiation quantity–unit pair is correctly matched?
x: Absorbed dose is measured in Gray; activity is in Becquerel and biological effect in Sievert.

s: What is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay called?
x: Half-life is the time for half the nuclei to decay.

s: In which unit is the biological effect of radiation on the human body expressed?
x: Sievert measures biological effect; gray is absorbed dose and becquerel is activity.

s: In which unit is the absorbed radiation dose of one joule per kilogram measured?
x: Gray (1 J/kg) is the unit of absorbed dose; becquerel measures activity and sievert biological effect.

s: What is BRIT (Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology)?
o: The regulator for radiation safety in India
An industrial unit of the Department of Atomic Energy for radioisotopes
A cancer hospital under the Ministry of Health
x: BRIT is an industrial unit of the DAE dealing with radioisotopes, radiopharmaceuticals and isotope technology.

s: Which is India's leading producer of radioisotopes?
x: BARC, set up as AEET in 1954 and renamed in 1967, is India's leading producer of radioisotopes.

s: Which is the largest research reactor of BARC?
x: Dhruva is the largest research reactor; Apsara was Asia's first and KAMINI is the only U-233-fuelled reactor.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about radioisotope production in India?
o: Research reactors at Trombay produce isotopes
NPCIL power plants play no part in isotope production
Isotopes are produced at reactors, an accelerator and power plants
x: India produces isotopes in Trombay research reactors, at the Kolkata accelerator and in NPCIL power plants, so saying NPCIL plants play no part is false.

s: The KRUSHAK facility at Lasalgaon is associated with the irradiation of which produce?
x: KRUSHAK at Lasalgaon in Nashik, Maharashtra, is an onion irradiation facility. Food irradiation helps control sprouting and extend shelf life.

s: What is ISOMED 2.0, completed in May 2025?
o: High-intensity gamma irradiator for sterilising healthcare products
x: ISOMED 2.0 is a high-intensity gamma irradiator for sterilising healthcare products, completed in May 2025.

s: In which year was BARC, set up as AEET in 1954, renamed?
x: AEET (1954) was renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in 1967.

s: Which BARC research reactor was Asia's first?
x: Apsara was Asia's first research reactor; Dhruva is BARC's largest and KAMINI the only U-233 reactor.

s: KAMINI is the only reactor fuelled by which isotope?
x: KAMINI is the only reactor using U-233 fuel.

s: Where is BRIT, the industrial unit of the Department of Atomic Energy, located?
x: BRIT is at Vashi, Navi Mumbai; Lasalgaon hosts the KRUSHAK onion irradiation facility.

s: On which effect is the conversion of decay heat into electricity by thermocouples in a radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG) based?
x: An RTG is not a fission reactor; its thermocouples turn decay heat directly into electricity by the Seebeck effect, so it has no moving parts.

s: Which isotope is generally used as fuel in radioisotope thermoelectric generators?
x: Plutonium-238 is the fuel commonly associated with RTGs. It has been described as a by-product of weapons-development programmes.

s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of spacecraft or planetary missions associated with the use of RTG power sources?
x: Voyager, Cassini and Curiosity are examples of missions using RTG power where sunlight is weak. Perseverance is another such example.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs)?
o: An RTG uses Plutonium-238 as fuel
An RTG has no moving parts
An RTG is a type of fission reactor
x: An RTG is not a fission reactor; it turns decay heat of Pu-238 into electricity.

s: The RTG fuel Plutonium-238 is obtained as a by-product of what?
x: Pu-238, not Pu-239, is the RTG fuel and is a by-product of weapons production.

s: Which sources are commonly used in gamma radiography for non-destructive testing of welds and castings?
x: Gamma radiography of welds and castings uses radiography cameras with sources such as Iridium-192 and Cobalt-60.

s:
Consider the following statements about food irradiation:
1. It works by radiolysis of water in the food.
2. Only Cobalt-60 gamma rays can be used as its source.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statement 1 is correct: food irradiation works by radiolysis of water. Statement 2 is wrong: the sources can be gamma rays (Co-60), X-rays or electron beams. So (b), (c) and (d) are wrong.

s: Who first demonstrated induced mutation in crop plants (barley) using X-rays?
x: L. J. Stadler first induced mutation in crop plants in 1928, using X-rays on barley. Gamma and neutron radiation were used later for mutation breeding.

s: TBM-9, a newer BARC Trombay variety developed with NRCB, Trichy, is a variety of which crop?
x: TBM-9 is the newer banana variety developed with NRCB, Trichy; RTS-43 is a sorghum variety.

s: In the sterile insect technique, radiation-sterilised males are released so that:
o: Mating with wild females produces no viable offspring
x: Gamma-sterilised males mate with wild females without producing viable offspring, so pest numbers decline.

s: What does the 'Radura' logo, an international symbol, indicate?
x: Radura is the international green symbol marking irradiated food. Organic, GM and fortified foods carry their own separate labels; Radura says only that the food was treated with radiation.

s: How many crop varieties have been developed using Trombay (BARC) technology?
x: 72 crop varieties have been developed by Trombay (BARC), a non-power use of nuclear technology that supports food security.

s: What are nuclear moisture gauges used to determine in agriculture?
x: Nuclear moisture gauges measure soil moisture and so help determine irrigation requirements.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about food irradiation in India?
o: Irradiation cannot be applied to bulk food
Irradiated mangoes have been exported to the United States
Irradiation can be carried out on packed food
x: Irradiation can be carried out on packed or bulk food.

s: RTS-43, a BARC Trombay variety, is a variety of which crop?
x: RTS-43 is a sorghum variety; TBM-9 is a banana variety.

s: Which radioisotope is used as a tracer to study fertiliser phosphorus uptake by plants?
x: P-32 is a fertiliser tracer for plant phosphorus uptake, besides its use in leukaemia.

s:
Consider the following statements about food irradiation:
1. It can use Cobalt-60 gamma rays, X-rays or electron beams.
2. It is the technique used to raise the genetic variety of crops.
3. It stops sprouting and kills pests.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Food irradiation uses Co-60 gamma, X-rays or electron beams to stop sprouting and kill pests; raising crop genetic variety is mutation breeding.

s: What is raising the genetic variety of crops by exposing them to radiation called?
x: Mutation breeding uses X-rays, gamma or neutron radiation to create new crop varieties.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about industrial uses of radiotracers?
o: They detect leaks in buried oil and gas pipelines
Sediment tracking at ports increases the frequency of desilting campaigns
They are used to study seepage from dams
They are used for flow measurement
x: Radiotracer tracking of sediment transport can help reduce, not increase, the frequency of desilting campaigns.

s: Which alpha emitter is commonly used in smoke detectors?
x: Smoke detectors use an alpha emitter, commonly Americium-241. The other listed isotopes are associated with RTGs or industrial and medical radiation applications.

s: In industry, Sodium-24 is used as a tracer to detect what?
x: Na-24 detects pipeline leaks; weld radiography uses Ir-192 or Co-60 and smoke detectors use Am-241.

s: Gamma rays from which radioisotope are commonly used for radiation sterilisation of medical products?
x: Co-60 gamma rays are used for sterilisation as well as cancer radiotherapy.

s: How do radiotracers that track sediment movement help at ports?
x: Radiotracer sediment tracking at ports cuts how often desilting is needed.

s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated effect or use of food irradiation?
o: Increasing the genetic diversity of crop seeds in the field
x: Food irradiation can stop sprouting, delay ripening and kill insects, parasites and pathogens. Increasing genetic diversity of field crops is associated with mutation breeding, not food irradiation.

s: Which of the following is a conventional source of energy?
x: Firewood is a conventional source; solar energy is non-conventional and wind energy renewable.

s: What are non-conventional sources of energy, by definition?
x: Non-conventional sources (solar, wind, etc.) are by definition renewable (UPPSC 2023 key). Non-renewable and fossil-based describe coal, oil and gas, which are conventional; 'imported' is not a classification of energy sources.

s: Which one of the following energy sources comes from the Earth's internal heat rather than from the Sun?
x: Geothermal energy comes from the Earth's internal heat; wind, hydro and biomass are stored solar energy.

s: Which of the following is a renewable resource?
x: Geothermal energy, like wind, is renewable; coal and nuclear fuels are finite, non-renewable resources.

s: Which of the following is non-fossil but NOT renewable?
x: Nuclear fuel is non-fossil but non-renewable (APPSC 2024); solar, geothermal and wind are renewable.

s: From which source is tidal energy mainly derived?
x: Tidal energy comes from the Moon, so like geothermal and nuclear it is not derived from the Sun.

s: Which of the following is conventional yet renewable?
x: Hydel is a conventional source but renewable; coal, petroleum and gas are conventional and non-renewable.

s: Which of the following is NOT a conventional form of energy?
x: Firewood, cattle-dung cake and hydel are conventional; solar is non-conventional.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Solar energy is the most important non-conventional energy source for India.
2. Solar power has been India's largest renewable source by installed capacity since 2014.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Solar is India's most important non-conventional source, but in 2014 wind (21 GW) was the largest renewable source; solar leads only now.

s: As of August 2026, which source formed the largest component of India's installed renewable-energy capacity?
x: Solar, at 164.59 GW (Aug 2026), is the largest RE component. Wind (58.14 GW) is second, large hydro is about 52 GW, and bio-power about 11.75 GW. In 2014 wind was the largest, but solar has overtaken it.

s: What share of India's electricity generation did renewable energy contribute in 2024–25?
x: Renewables were about half of installed capacity but supplied only about 22% of generation; coal and thermal gave about 75%.

s: Which was the second-largest renewable-energy type by installed capacity in India as of August 2026?
x: Wind (58.14 GW) is second after solar (164.59 GW); large hydro is about 52 GW.

s: What was India's large hydro installed capacity in August 2026?
x: Large hydro is about 52 GW; wind is 58.14 GW and bio-power about 11.75 GW.

s: What share of India's electricity generation did coal and thermal power provide in 2024-25?
x: Coal/thermal gave about 75% of generation while renewables gave only about 22%.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched with cumulative installed capacity in 2014?
x: In 2014, cumulative solar capacity was 2.8 GW and wind capacity was 21 GW. Wind was then the largest renewable source.

s: When did India's installed wind capacity cross 50 GW?
x: Wind crossed 50 GW in March 2025.

s: In 2014-15, which was the next-largest renewable-energy type by installed capacity after wind?
x: In 2014-15 wind (23.44 GW) led, followed by bio-power at 8.55 GW.

s:
Consider the following statements:
1. India's cumulative installed solar capacity was 63.30 GW on 31 December 2022.
2. In 2014, solar was India's largest renewable source by installed capacity.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Solar capacity was 63.30 GW on 31 December 2022; in 2014 wind (21 GW) was the largest RE source, solar was only 2.8 GW.

s: To whom does the Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO) apply?
o: DISCOMs and large or designated consumers
x: RPO requires DISCOMs and large or designated consumers to procure a prescribed share of power from renewables.

s: The Solar Renewable Purchase Obligation was raised to what level by March 2022?
x: The Solar RPO trajectory raised the solar obligation to 8% by March 2022.

s: Under the Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act, 2022, the Renewable Purchase Obligation has been recast as an obligation to do what?
x: RPO concerns purchase of renewable power; the RCO recasts it as an obligation to consume renewable energy under the 2022 amendment.

s: Who builds the Inter-State Green Energy Corridor lines that evacuate renewable power to load centres?
x: Inter-State GEC lines are built by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (PGCIL).

s: Which of the following pairs is INCORRECTLY matched (State – Intra-State GEC-I)?
x: GEC-I covered AP, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu; Telangana was not one of the eight.

s: What was the financing pattern for Intra-State GEC-I?
o: MNRE 50%, KfW loan 25% and State utility 25%
MNRE 20%, KfW loan 40% and State utility 40%
MNRE 40%, KfW loan 20% and State utility 40%
MNRE 40%, KfW loan 40% and State utility 20%
x: The cost-sharing pattern was MNRE 40%, KfW of Germany loan 40% and State utility contribution 20%.

s: Green Energy Corridor Phase-II (2022) covers how many States?
x: GEC-II covers 7 States and about 20 GW of RE; GEC-I covered 8 States.

s: From which lender did the 40% loan component of Intra-State GEC-I come?
x: GEC-I was funded MNRE 40% : KfW (Germany) loan 40% : State utility 20%.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Green Energy Corridor (GEC)?
o: It has been under way since 2015
Andhra Pradesh is among the 8 States of Intra-State GEC-I
Tamil Nadu is among the 8 States of Intra-State GEC-I
Odisha is among the 8 States of Intra-State GEC-I
x: Intra-State GEC-I covers AP, Gujarat, HP, Karnataka, MP, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu; Odisha is not among them.

s: Which of the following States is NOT part of the Intra-State Green Energy Corridor-I?
x: Odisha is not in Intra-State GEC-I; AP, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu are.

s: What is the Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Limited (IREDA)?
o: A commercial bank under the Ministry of Finance
An NBFC under the administrative control of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy
A statutory regulator under the Ministry of Power
A non-governmental organisation under the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
x: IREDA is an NBFC under the administrative control of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE).

s: Which of the following is NOT a function of IREDA?
o: Determining statutory electricity tariffs for all States
Providing term, bridge and working-capital loans
x: IREDA undertakes project financing, appraisal, consultancy and provides term, bridge and working-capital loans. Determination of statutory tariffs for all States is not its function.

s: When was IREDA granted Navratna status?
x: IREDA became a Navratna in April 2024, after listing in November 2023.

s: When was IREDA listed on the NSE and BSE?
x: IREDA listed on 29 November 2023 and got Navratna status in April 2024.

s: The National Clean Energy Fund (NCEF) was financed by a cess levied on which of the following?
x: The NCEF, announced in the 2010-11 Budget, was financed by the Clean Energy Cess on coal, lignite and peat.

s: For what purpose was the National Clean Energy Fund (NCEF) created in 2010-11?
o: To fund research and innovative projects in clean energy technologies
To pay compensation for nuclear accidents
x: The NCEF was set up to fund research and innovative projects in clean energy and renewable energy, to cut dependence on fossil fuels.

s: The original target of 175 GW renewable-energy capacity by 2022 consisted of which combination?
o: 75 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 30 GW bio-power and 10 GW small hydro
60 GW solar, 100 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro
100 GW solar, 50 GW wind, 20 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro
100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro
x: The 175 GW target comprised 100 GW solar, 60 GW wind, 10 GW bio-power and 5 GW small hydro. The target was not achieved on time and was later superseded.

s:
Consider the following statements about India's non-fossil capacity targets:
1. The 2015 NDC set a target of 40% non-fossil capacity by 2030.
2. India achieved 50% non-fossil installed capacity in June 2025, five years ahead of schedule.
3. The 50% non-fossil target was set by the 2015 NDC.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: Statements 1 and 2 are true. The 50% target came from the updated NDC and COP26 Panchamrit, not the 2015 NDC.

s: Which one of the following pairs correctly states India's 2030 and 2070 energy commitments?
o: 500 GW renewable capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2050
300 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2070
500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2060
500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030 and Net Zero by 2070
x: India's stated commitments include 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and achieving Net Zero by 2070.

s:
Consider the following statements about India's renewable-energy targets:
1. The target of 175 GW renewable capacity by 2022 was achieved.
2. India's Net Zero target year is 2070.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
x: The 175 GW by 2022 target was missed and replaced; Net Zero is set for 2070.

s: What is India's target for non-fossil installed capacity by 2030?
x: The target is 500 GW non-fossil by 2030; about 300 GW was reached in 2026.

s: Which target – commitment pair is correctly matched?
x: The 2015 NDC set 40%; Panchamrit set 50%; Net Zero is 2070 and 175 GW was for 2022.

s: What is India's global rank in installed wind-power capacity?
x: India ranks 4th in the world in wind power, while it is 3rd in total renewable capacity after China and the USA. China ranks first; India is neither second nor as low as tenth.

s: Of India's estimated solar potential of 748 GW, about what share had been utilised?
x: India's solar potential is estimated at 748 GW, of which only about 4.5% had been utilised.

s: According to IRENA 2026 rankings, India stood at which position globally in renewable-energy capacity?
x: India ranked third in renewable-energy capacity after China and the United States. The stated capacities were China 2,258 GW, the USA 468 GW and India 250.5 GW.

s: Which State was the leading renewable-energy State, with 42.58 GW and 16.5% of India's renewable capacity in June 2026?
x: Gujarat was the leading renewable-energy State in June 2026, with 42.58 GW and 16.5% of India's renewable capacity.

s: Which State has the highest share (23.70%) of India's renewable-energy potential?
x: Rajasthan has the top RE potential; Gujarat has the top installed capacity.

s: Which State leads India in installed wind capacity?
x: Gujarat leads both total installed RE capacity and wind capacity.

s: What was India's renewable-energy capacity according to IRENA 2026?
x: India had 250.5 GW (3rd), behind China (2,258 GW) and the USA (468 GW).

s: Which is the dominant solar-cell technology in the market?
x: Crystalline silicon (mono- and polycrystalline) cells dominate the market; thin-film cells are cheaper and flexible but less efficient.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about solar thermal (concentrated solar power) technology?
o: Mirrors may concentrate sunlight to heat a fluid
Solar power towers are associated with solar thermal applications
The heat can produce steam for a turbine
Heat storage is not possible in such systems
x: Solar thermal systems can store heat; they collect or concentrate solar heat for water, steam and power generation.

s: In a solar PV system, which device converts the DC produced by the cells into AC for the grid?
x: PV cells produce direct current; an inverter converts it to alternating current. A transformer only changes voltage.

s: What is the capacity-utilisation factor of solar power in India?
x: The stated CUFs are about 21% for solar, 36–40% for wind and about 85% for coal.

s: How do thin-film solar cells (CdTe, CIGS, a-Si) compare with crystalline silicon cells?
x: Thin-film cells are cheaper and bendable but less efficient; crystalline silicon dominates.

s: What efficiency did the perovskite-silicon tandem cell developed by IIT Bombay under an MNRE project reach?
x: The tandem cell reached 30.2%; the single perovskite cell reached 26%.

s: From which source do artificial satellites get their electricity?
x: Satellites use solar (photovoltaic) cells that turn sunlight directly into electricity.

s: Modhera in Gujarat is recognised as India's first:
x: Modhera, the Sun Temple town in Mehsana district, became India's first 24x7 solar-powered village.

s: Which is the world's first fully solar-powered airport?
x: Cochin International Airport is the world's first fully solar-powered airport.

s: Which is India's first all-solar-kitchen village?
x: Bancha (Betul, MP) is the first all-solar-kitchen village; Modhera is the 24x7 solar village.

s: Where is India's first National Centre for Marine Biodiversity located?
x: India's first National Centre for Marine Biodiversity is at Jamnagar, near the Gulf of Kachchh Marine National Park.

s: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
o: Jim Corbett National Park was established in 1936.
India’s first National Park was established in 1984.
The First Rhino Rehabilitation Programme was conducted at Dudhwa National Park in 1984.
The original name of Jim Corbett National Park was Hailey National Park.
x: Option B is incorrect: India's first national park, Corbett (first named Hailey), dates from 1936. 1984 is the first rhino rehabilitation at Dudhwa.

s:
Assertion (A): Seshachalam is the first Biosphere Reserve of Andhra Pradesh.
Reason (R): Surat was the first district with 100% solar-powered primary health centres.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
x: Both statements are true, but they are unrelated, so R does not explain A.

s: In which year was the first World Climate Conference held?
x: The first World Climate Conference was in 1979; the first Earth Summit was at Rio in 1992.

s: Which was the first Union Territory of India to run fully on solar power during the day?
x: Diu became the first city/UT to run 100% on solar power by day, with plants installed in 2018.

s: At which two Indian cities did the solar-powered aircraft Solar Impulse 2 halt in March 2015?
x: Solar Impulse 2 stopped at Ahmedabad and Varanasi in March 2015 on its round-the-world flight.

s: Where was the first Earth Summit, which adopted Agenda 21, held in 1992?
x: The first Earth Summit was held at Rio de Janeiro in 1992 and adopted Agenda 21.

s: The International Solar Alliance (ISA) was launched at which place and event?
o: Gwal Pahari during the laying of the headquarters foundation stone
New Delhi during the founding conference of ISA
x: The ISA was launched jointly by India and France on 30 November 2015 at COP21 in Paris.

s: When did the Framework Agreement of the International Solar Alliance enter into force?
x: The ISA Framework Agreement entered into force on 6 December 2017, giving the organisation its treaty-based character.

s: Which of the following initiatives was launched at the 8th Assembly of the International Solar Alliance held in New Delhi?
x: The Global SIDS Initiative, ISA Academy, Global Capability Centre and SUNRISE were launched at the 8th ISA Assembly in New Delhi.

s: Which initiative of the International Solar Alliance is intended to share solar power across time zones through a transnational grid?
x: OSOWOG, or One Sun One World One Grid, is the transnational grid concept for sharing solar power across time zones.

s: What does the Global Solar Facility of the ISA mainly seek to do?
o: Produce green hydrogen from solar power
Train solar engineers in member countries
De-risk solar investment in underserved regions
x: The Global Solar Facility is an ISA fund designed to de-risk solar investment in underserved regions through instruments such as payment guarantees and insurance.

s: How much solar investment does the International Solar Alliance aim to mobilise?
x: The ISA's stated goal is to mobilise $1 trillion of solar investment by 2030.

s: Which of the following pairs is correctly matched?
o: OSOWOG — Pooling demand for bulk procurement of solar equipment
Common procurement platform — Pooling demand to reduce costs through scale
ISA Academy — Treaty-making body of the ISA
x: The common procurement platform pools demand so that costs can be reduced through economies of scale. OSOWOG concerns an interconnected solar grid, while STAR-C concerns training and best practices.

s: How many member countries does the International Solar Alliance have?
x: ISA has 112 members (not 38), with 116+ signatories; 137 nations attended the 8th Assembly.

s: Which country most recently ratified the ISA, in March 2026?
x: Romania is the newest member, having ratified in March 2026.

s: Where was the foundation stone of the ISA headquarters laid on 25 January 2016?
x: PM Modi and President Hollande laid it at the NISE campus, Gwal Pahari, Gurugram.

s: In which region does the first guarantee programme of the ISA Global Solar Facility with MIGA (Sept 2024) start?
x: The MIGA-ISA Solar Facility starts in Sub-Saharan Africa; the ADB pact (2018) covers Asia and the Pacific.

s: Which one of the following is NOT an initiative of the International Solar Alliance?
o: One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG)
x: PM-KUSUM is a domestic MNRE scheme for solarising farm power, not an ISA project. OSOWOG (transnational solar grid), STAR-C (knowledge and training centres) and the Global Solar Facility (de-risking fund) are ISA initiatives.

s: Which ISA initiative – purpose pair is correctly matched?
o: OSOWOG – Fund to de-risk solar investment
Global Solar Facility – Transnational solar grid
x: STAR-C is for training and knowledge; OSOWOG is the grid and the Global Solar Facility de-risks investment.

s: Which is the first treaty-based intergovernmental organisation headquartered in India?
x: The ISA, with its headquarters at Gurugram, is the first treaty-based intergovernmental body headquartered in India.

s:
Match the following:
List-I (ISA event)
A. Launch of the ISA
B. Foundation stone of the ISA headquarters
C. Founding conference of the ISA
List-II (Place)
1. Gurugram
2. Paris
3. New Delhi
Select the correct answer using the code given below.
x: ISA was launched at COP21 in Paris (2015), its HQ foundation stone was laid at Gwal Pahari, Gurugram (2016), and its founding conference was held in New Delhi (2018).

s: India added a record solar capacity of approximately how much in financial year 2025-26?
x: A record 44.61 GW of solar capacity was added in FY 2025-26. The 2.82 GW figure relates to the earlier 2014 level, while about 38 GW refers to the 2025 addition in another comparison.

s: How much solar capacity did India add in 2025, beating the US for the first time?
x: India added about 38 GW in 2025, becoming the second-largest solar growth market and overtaking the US for the first time.

s: Which State had the largest installed solar capacity in April 2026?
x: Rajasthan has led solar since 2021: 41,012 MW on 31 Mar 2026, against Gujarat's 29,303 MW. Gujarat (about 47 GW) leads only total RE capacity and rooftop solar.

s: Which country is the world's largest solar producer and the first to pass 1 TW of solar capacity?
x: China is the largest solar producer and first to cross 1 TW (2025); India is 3rd.

s: What was India's cumulative installed solar capacity in 2014?
x: Solar was 2.82 GW in 2014, rising to 63.30 GW by 31 December 2022.

s: What was India's installed solar capacity in August 2026, about 29 per cent of total installed capacity?
x: Installed solar capacity reached 164.59 GW in August 2026, about 29 per cent of India's total capacity. 150.26 GW was the 31 March 2026 figure and 44.61 GW the record addition in 2025-26.

s: What is India's global rank in installed solar capacity (2025-26)?
x: India is third in the world in solar capacity; China is first.

s: Which is the State nodal agency for solar development in Andhra Pradesh?
x: NEDCAP is the State nodal agency for Andhra Pradesh's solar programme; SECI and MNRE have national-level roles.

s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Andhra Pradesh's solar-energy cluster?
o: Kurnool and YSR Kadapa parks anchor the Rayalaseema renewable-energy cluster
NTPC Simhadri has a floating solar plant in Visakhapatnam
SECI is the State nodal agency
About 50,000 acres of barren land have been offered for solar lease
x: NEDCAP, not SECI, is the nodal agency for Andhra Pradesh's solar programme.

s: Which of the following is reported to be still absent in India's solar sector?
o: An approved list of module manufacturers (ALMM)
x: Solar-waste recycling norms are still absent; cell capacity lag and grid curtailment are other concerns.

s: Since which year has the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) for solar been compulsory?
x: ALMM has been compulsory since 2019 and covers government-funded and government-linked projects such as PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM and SECI tenders, not only private projects.

s: From when does ALMM List-III for ingots and wafers become mandatory?
x: List-III becomes mandatory only from June 2028; List-II for cells (ALCM) applies from 1 June 2026.

s: Which of the following pairs of Basic Customs Duty rates is correctly matched with solar imports from April 2022?
x: From April 2022, the Basic Customs Duty was 40 per cent on modules and 25 per cent on cells.

s: How much manufacturing capacity does the ALMM module list cover?
